stem: A company wants its stored files to survive the loss of an entire data center without any extra configuration.
prompt: Which AWS storage choice provides this by default?

options.text: Amazon S3 Standard
options.why: S3 Standard stores data redundantly across at least three Availability Zones by default.

options.text: A local disk on an on-premises server
options.why: Local disks offer no protection against a data center loss.

options.text: An EC2 instance store volume
options.why: Instance store data is lost when the instance stops or fails.

options.text: An Amazon EBS volume in one Availability Zone
options.why: EBS volumes are replicated within a single AZ, not across AZs.

explanation.answer: Amazon S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability by storing objects across multiple AZs.
explanation.concept: Different storage services have different durability and availability designs.
explanation.examTip: Survive an AZ loss by default = Amazon S3 (multi-AZ storage classes).

stem: A colleague asks what "managed service" means on AWS.
prompt: Which description is BEST?

options.text: AWS staff monitor your users' activity for you
options.why: AWS does not monitor your users on your behalf.

options.text: AWS operates the underlying infrastructure and routine tasks for you
options.why: With managed services, AWS handles tasks such as provisioning, patching and backups.

options.text: AWS manages your application code and business logic
options.why: Customers remain responsible for their code and data.

options.text: A service that only runs inside your own data center
options.why: Managed services run on AWS infrastructure.

explanation.answer: A managed service is one where AWS takes on operational tasks such as provisioning, patching, scaling and backups, so you focus on using it.
explanation.concept: Examples include Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3.
explanation.examTip: Managed = AWS runs the plumbing; you own your data and configuration.

stem: Before migrating, a company inventories its 300 applications and assigns each one a migration strategy.
prompt: What is the main benefit of this step?

options.text: It lets AWS migrate the applications automatically
options.why: AWS provides tools, but the customer plans and runs the migration.

options.text: It removes the need to test applications after migration
options.why: Testing is still required after migration.

options.text: It matches effort to value for each application
options.why: Choosing a strategy per application balances effort, cost and benefit.

options.text: It ensures every application cuts over without downtime
options.why: Planning reduces risk but can't ensure zero downtime.

explanation.answer: Portfolio assessment assigns each application to one of the 7 Rs based on business value, complexity and constraints.
explanation.concept: Not every application deserves the same effort: some are retired, some rehosted, some refactored.
explanation.examTip: Assign a strategy per app = portfolio assessment.

stem: A company is unsure whether it will move from EC2 to AWS Fargate and Lambda next year but still wants a discount for its steady compute use.
prompt: Which option keeps the MOST flexibility?

options.text: Standard Reserved Instances for specific instance types
options.why: Standard RIs are tied to instance attributes and don't cover Fargate or Lambda.

options.text: Spot Instances for all steady workloads
options.why: Spot can be interrupted and is not a commitment discount.

options.text: Dedicated Hosts with a three-year reservation
options.why: Host reservations lock in physical servers.

options.text: Compute Savings Plans
options.why: Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda, regardless of instance family or Region.

explanation.answer: Compute Savings Plans offer discounts in exchange for a dollar-per-hour commitment that applies across EC2, AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda.
explanation.concept: EC2 Instance Savings Plans give deeper discounts but are tied to an instance family in a Region.
explanation.examTip: Discount + flexibility across EC2, Fargate, Lambda = Compute Savings Plans.

stem: A web application stores user session data on each web server. When a server is replaced, users get logged out.
prompt: Which change BEST follows cloud design principles?

options.text: Store session state outside the servers
options.why: Stateless servers can be added or replaced without affecting users.

options.text: Use one web server so sessions stay on it
options.why: A single server is a single point of failure.

options.text: Keep the same web servers running permanently
options.why: Servers must be replaceable for scaling and recovery.

options.text: Copy session files to each server by hand
options.why: Manual copying is error-prone and doesn't scale.

explanation.answer: Making servers stateless, by moving session state to a shared store, lets you scale and replace servers freely.
explanation.concept: Stateless design supports horizontal scaling and disposable resources.
explanation.examTip: Users logged out when servers change = move state off the servers.

stem: A company wants to test demand for its product in Australia before committing to a long-term presence.
prompt: Which AWS characteristic makes this low-risk?

options.text: Long-term hardware contracts in each country
options.why: Long-term contracts increase risk for a test.

options.text: Deploying to a nearby Region on demand and shutting it down anytime
options.why: The company can launch in a nearby Region, test, and stop paying if demand is low.

options.text: Shipping servers to Australia with AWS Snowball
options.why: Snowball moves data; it doesn't host production applications.

options.text: Mandatory one-year commitments per Region
options.why: There are no mandatory commitments to use a Region.

explanation.answer: With on-demand Regions, companies can expand globally to test markets without long-term investment.
explanation.concept: Going global in minutes reduces the risk of entering new markets.
explanation.examTip: Test a new market cheaply = deploy in a nearby Region on demand.

stem: AWS CAF describes a cloud transformation journey in phases.
prompt: Which sequence lists these phases in order?

options.text: Discover, Design, Deploy, Decommission
options.why: These are not the AWS CAF phases, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Migrate, Assess, Optimize, Retire
options.why: These are not the AWS CAF phases, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Envision, Align, Launch, Scale
options.why: AWS CAF describes the transformation journey as Envision, Align, Launch and Scale.

options.text: Plan, Build, Run, Retire
options.why: These are generic project phases, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: AWS CAF's transformation journey has four iterative phases: Envision, Align, Launch and Scale.
explanation.concept: Envision opportunities, align stakeholders, launch pilots and scale them to production.
explanation.examTip: CAF phases: Envision → Align → Launch → Scale.

references.title: Overview of the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework

stem: A company is migrating a three-tier application: web servers on VMs and an Oracle database that will become Amazon RDS for Oracle.
prompt: Which combination of services fits BEST?

options.text: AWS DataSync for the servers and AWS Backup for the database
options.why: DataSync moves files, and AWS Backup does not migrate databases.

options.text: Amazon S3 for the VMs and Amazon Athena for the database
options.why: S3 and Athena are not migration services.

options.text: AWS Snowball Edge for both tiers
options.why: Snowball moves data offline but does not rehost servers or replicate database changes.

options.text: Application Migration Service for the VMs and AWS DMS for the database
options.why: MGN rehosts the servers, and DMS moves the data into the managed database.

explanation.answer: Rehosting servers with AWS Application Migration Service and migrating the database with AWS DMS is a common pattern.
explanation.concept: Use the right tool per layer: servers, databases and files have different migration services.
explanation.examTip: Servers → MGN. Databases → DMS. Files → DataSync. Offline bulk → Snowball.

references.title: What is AWS Application Migration Service?

stem: A finance team complains that on premises it was hard to know what each application cost.
prompt: How does AWS improve this?

options.text: Usage-based billing with tags and detailed cost reports
options.why: Costs are recorded per resource and usage, and tags let teams attribute them.

options.text: AWS charges a single flat fee per account
options.why: AWS charges by usage, not a flat fee, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: AWS assigns a cost to each employee automatically
options.why: AWS does not attribute costs to employees.

options.text: AWS hides costs until the end of the year
options.why: AWS provides near-real-time cost data, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: On AWS, every resource's usage is metered. Cost allocation tags and tools like AWS Cost Explorer show costs by application, team or project.
explanation.concept: Cost visibility supports accountability and optimization.
explanation.examTip: Who spends what = metered billing + tags + Cost Explorer.

stem: An architect says: "Everything fails all the time, so design for it."
prompt: Which practice reflects this mindset?

options.text: Avoiding monitoring to reduce noise
options.why: Monitoring is needed to detect failures.

options.text: Building redundancy and automatic recovery into the workload
options.why: Assuming failure leads to redundancy across AZs and automated recovery.

options.text: Running everything in one data center for simplicity
options.why: One location is a single point of failure.

options.text: Buying the most expensive hardware available
options.why: Even expensive hardware fails, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: Designing for failure means expecting components to fail and building in redundancy, health checks and automated recovery.
explanation.concept: Multiple AZs, load balancers and Auto Scaling are common tools for this.
explanation.examTip: Assume failure: redundancy + automatic recovery.

stem: A company needs extra compute for a two-week marketing campaign each year.
prompt: What is the MOST cost-effective approach on AWS?

options.text: Buy servers sized for the campaign and keep them all year
options.why: Owning idle servers for 50 weeks wastes money.

options.text: Purchase a Dedicated Host for the campaign
options.why: Dedicated Hosts add cost and aren't needed here.

options.text: Launch On-Demand capacity for the two weeks only
options.why: On-Demand lets the company pay for the campaign weeks and nothing afterwards.

options.text: Sign a one-year Reserved Instance for campaign capacity
options.why: A one-year commitment charges for capacity used only two weeks.

explanation.answer: On-Demand pricing suits short, unpredictable or temporary workloads with no long-term commitment.
explanation.concept: Commitments save money only when usage is steady over the term.
explanation.examTip: Short-term spike = On-Demand (or Spot if interruptible).

stem: A CAF workshop lists these concerns: data architecture, platform engineering and CI/CD.
prompt: Which perspective owns these capabilities?

options.text: Business
options.why: Business covers strategy and outcomes, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Operations
options.why: Operations covers running services, such as observability and incident management.

options.text: Governance
options.why: Governance covers risk, benefits and financial management.

options.text: Platform
options.why: Platform includes platform architecture, data architecture, platform engineering, provisioning and modern app development.

explanation.answer: The Platform perspective helps build an enterprise-grade cloud platform, including CI/CD and data architecture.
explanation.concept: Technical perspectives: Platform (build), Security (protect), Operations (run).
explanation.examTip: Build the platform = Platform. Protect = Security. Run = Operations.

stem: A company wants to recreate its entire production environment in another Region quickly and exactly.
prompt: Which practice makes this MOST achievable?

options.text: Define infrastructure as code templates
options.why: Templates can deploy the same environment in any Region repeatedly.

options.text: Document each console click in a wiki
options.why: Manual steps from a wiki are slow and error-prone.

options.text: Take screenshots of current settings
options.why: Screenshots can't recreate resources, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Ask AWS Support to copy the environment
options.why: AWS Support doesn't copy customer environments.

explanation.answer: Infrastructure as code (for example AWS CloudFormation) lets you provision identical environments quickly in any Region.
explanation.concept: IaC supports disaster recovery, consistency and auditability.
explanation.examTip: Recreate exactly, anywhere = infrastructure as code.

stem: A company wants better price performance for its Linux web servers without changing its architecture much.
prompt: Which option should it evaluate?

options.text: Moving the servers back on premises
options.why: Going back on premises adds hardware costs.

options.text: AWS Graviton-based EC2 instances
options.why: Graviton instances can deliver better price performance for many Linux workloads.

options.text: Dedicated Hosts for every web server
options.why: Dedicated Hosts add cost and are for licensing or compliance.

options.text: Switching to the largest x86 instance type
options.why: Larger instances raise cost; they don't improve price performance by themselves.

explanation.answer: AWS Graviton processors are designed by AWS to deliver strong price performance and energy efficiency for many workloads.
explanation.concept: Many Linux applications run on Graviton with little or no change.
explanation.examTip: Better price performance for Linux = try Graviton.

stem: A small business wants to start using cloud servers today without signing contracts or paying anything upfront.
prompt: Which statement is TRUE about AWS?

options.text: AWS requires an upfront deposit for new accounts
options.why: Most services have no upfront payment, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: AWS requires a one-year minimum contract
options.why: There is no minimum contract for most services.

options.text: Most services can be used with no upfront commitment
options.why: On-Demand use is pay-as-you-go with no long-term contract.

options.text: AWS only sells capacity in yearly blocks
options.why: Capacity is available on demand by the second or hour.

explanation.answer: AWS offers pay-as-you-go pricing with no upfront commitment for most services. Commitments are optional and give discounts.
explanation.concept: Optional commitments include Savings Plans and Reserved Instances.
explanation.examTip: No contracts required; commitments are optional discounts.

stem: A company completed a Well-Architected review a year ago and has since added many new features.
prompt: What does AWS recommend?

options.text: Treat the first review as final for the workload
options.why: Reviews should be repeated as workloads change.

options.text: Wait until a major outage before reviewing again
options.why: Reviews should prevent incidents, not follow them.

options.text: Replace the workload with a new one
options.why: Reviews improve workloads; they don't require replacing them.

options.text: Review again regularly and at key milestones
options.why: Regular reviews catch new risks as the architecture evolves.

explanation.answer: Well-Architected reviews should happen regularly and at important milestones, because architectures change over time.
explanation.concept: The review is a conversation, not an audit, and results feed an improvement plan.
explanation.examTip: Architecture changed = review again.

references.title: What is the AWS Well-Architected Tool?

stem: A company is considering refactoring an application during migration.
prompt: Which situation BEST justifies the extra effort of refactoring?

options.text: The business needs features the current design can't support
options.why: A strong need for agility or scale is the main reason to re-architect.

options.text: The application is no longer used by anyone
options.why: Unused applications should be retired, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: The application must stay on premises for compliance
options.why: That situation calls for retaining it, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: The data center lease ends next month
options.why: A short deadline favors rehosting, not refactoring.

explanation.answer: Refactoring is justified when the business needs capabilities that are hard to achieve in the existing architecture, such as scaling or faster feature delivery.
explanation.concept: Refactoring is the most expensive strategy upfront but can deliver the largest long-term benefit.
explanation.examTip: Refactor when business needs demand it, not when time is short.

stem: A company is explaining to its board why moving to AWS can lower costs over time.
prompt: Which TWO reasons are valid? (Select TWO.)

options.text: AWS caps each customer's bill at last year's level
options.why: AWS doesn't cap bills; costs depend on usage.

options.text: Data transfer out of AWS has no charge
options.why: Data transfer out is generally charged, so it doesn't fit this scenario.

options.text: AWS passes on savings from its economies of scale
options.why: AWS has lowered prices many times as its scale grew.

options.text: AWS covers the cost of the company's IT staff
options.why: AWS does not pay customer staff, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: The company pays only for what it uses
options.why: Pay-as-you-go eliminates paying for idle capacity.

explanation.answer: Economies of scale and pay-as-you-go pricing are two main reasons the cloud can reduce costs.
explanation.concept: Total savings depend on rightsizing, choosing pricing models and removing waste.
explanation.examTip: Lower costs: scale + pay-as-you-go. Watch for "always free" or "guaranteed" distractors.

stem: A company splits a large application into small services that teams can deploy independently.
prompt: Which benefit does this MOST directly provide?

options.text: Lower data transfer costs between all components
options.why: Microservices often add network calls; data transfer isn't the main benefit.

options.text: Faster, independent releases with smaller blast radius
options.why: Small services can be changed and deployed independently, and a failure in one affects less.

options.text: No need for monitoring or logging
options.why: Distributed services need more monitoring, not less.

options.text: Automatic compliance certification
options.why: Architecture style doesn't certify compliance.

explanation.answer: Microservices let teams release independently and isolate failures, which improves agility and reliability.
explanation.concept: They pair well with containers, serverless and loose coupling.
explanation.examTip: Independent deploys + smaller blast radius = microservices.

stem: A hospital must keep certain patient systems on premises but wants to use AWS for analytics.
prompt: Which deployment model allows this?

options.text: On-premises only
options.why: On-premises only wouldn't use AWS for analytics.

options.text: Single-tenant SaaS
options.why: This is a software delivery model, not a way to combine on-premises and AWS.

options.text: Hybrid
options.why: Hybrid connects on-premises systems with cloud services.

options.text: Cloud-only
options.why: Cloud-only would require moving the on-premises systems.

explanation.answer: A hybrid deployment model connects on-premises infrastructure with AWS, so some systems stay local while others use the cloud.
explanation.concept: Connectivity options include AWS Site-to-Site VPN and AWS Direct Connect.
explanation.examTip: Must keep some things on premises + use AWS = hybrid.
